claims.text: Residual interfacial strain and nanoscale defect structures primarily govern the magnetocaloric response of non-equiatomic FeMnNiGeSi thin films and nanoribbons.
Residual interfacial strain and nanoscale defect structures primarily govern low-field magnetic hysteresis in these films and nanoribbons.
As-deposited FeMnNiGeSi films and nanoribbons possess significant tensile or compressive residual strain and high densities of grain boundaries and dislocations.
The as-deposited nanoscale material has a broad distribution of local magnetic anisotropies.
Low-dimensional or nanostructured forms can exhibit a lower magnetocaloric response than corresponding bulk material.
The magnetocaloric entropy-change feature is broadened in low-dimensional FeMnNiGeSi relative to bulk specimens.
Moderate post-deposition annealing can relieve residual strain and reduce or reorder the defect network without excessive grain growth or phase separation.
Strain- and defect-induced variations in magnetic anisotropy broaden the magnetic transition.
Strain and defects promote magnetic hysteresis by impeding coherent domain switching.
Interfacial strain and defects slow thermal diffusion in as-deposited FeMnNiGeSi films and nanoribbons.
Annealing-induced strain relief will sharpen the magnetic transition.
Annealing will produce a larger and more temperature-confined magnetic entropy change.
Changes in the magnitude and shape of the magnetic entropy-change curve affect magnetocaloric refrigeration performance.
Annealed samples will have a higher peak magnetic entropy change than as-deposited samples under the same low-field conditions.
Annealed samples will have narrower low-field hysteresis loops than as-deposited samples.
Reducing internal strain will improve thermal equilibration and cycling reproducibility.
The proposed mechanism applies to films or patterned nanoribbons with feature dimensions typically below 100 nm, at fields below 0.1 T and near the magnetic transition.
Cycling beyond the heat-transfer-rate limit can cause deviations from the predicted behavior.
Direct mechanistic evidence for strain-controlled magnetocaloric behavior in low-dimensional FeMnNiGeSi is limited.
